1: Module context: The Influence module equips participants to understand how each CXO role transforms strategic intent into execution reality. In this phase, leaders move from being architects of strategy to engineers of execution flow: unclogging resistance and establishing the accountability architecture required to sustain momentum under pressure.

Throughout this module, participants explore how different functional perspectives interpret direction, and identify the specific steps where these interpretations create either cross-functional tension or powerful reinforcement.
4: The central problem (activity and progress): Performance Management Setup creates the visibility infrastructure that allows your organisation to see whether the work being done is actually moving the Key Results forward. Surveillance and pressure have no place in it.

Most organisations confuse activity with progress. People are busy. Initiatives are running. Reports are produced. Yet the fundamental question (are we closer to the Success in Practice today than we were last month?) is rarely answered with confidence.

This setup is about creating the infrastructure that answers that question with confidence. It is the leadership discipline of monitoring strategy in real time: how leaders decide whether to stay the course, pivot, or double down, based on hard evidence.

The goal of this section: to shift the perspective of your team. Performance management is often dreaded because it is viewed as a policing tool. We need to reframe it as the visibility infrastructure of organisational progress toward the Success in Practice.

Facilitator framing: When you introduce Performance Management Setup, ask leaders to clear their minds of the words “surveillance” and “pressure”. Ask them to picture the dashboard of a high-performance vehicle. A dashboard gives the driver accurate, real-time information so that they can make better decisions: whether to accelerate, adjust course, or pull over and refuel. It passes no judgement on the driver. The Performance Management system is the organisational equivalent: the visibility infrastructure of strategy execution.
5: Why the distinction comes first: Before exploring how to design a Performance Management system, leaders must first resolve a confusion that undermines execution in most organisations. The terms performance measurement and performance management are routinely used as if they mean the same thing, and treating them as interchangeable is one of the most common reasons that well-designed scorecards produce no change in execution.

Performance measurement in full: Performance measurement is the act of collecting, tracking, and interpreting data about results. It provides the evidence of what has occurred. A measurement system captures complaint resolution times, decision cycle durations, collaboration rates, revenue attainment, customer satisfaction scores: the numbers that describe organisational reality at a given point in time.

Performance management in full: Performance management is the broader leadership discipline of using that data, combined with accountability structures, deliberate conversations, and timely decisions, to shape what happens next. It reaches beyond any report or dashboard: it is the leadership response to what measurement reveals. It answers a different and more consequential question than measurement does.
Measurement is an input. Management is the response. One without the other produces either data without direction, or instinct without evidence.

A critical distinction for every leader: Many organisations invest heavily in measurement infrastructure (dashboards, platforms, KPI libraries) and very little in management discipline. The result is that data exists in abundance, but the conversations, decisions, and interventions that should follow from that data never materialise. Leaders look at numbers. The numbers do not change the work.
The purpose of the Performance Management Setup in S2R® is to build both: a rigorous measurement architecture and a leadership management discipline that converts data into execution momentum.
6: What comes first: Neither measurement nor management comes first. Both are downstream of something more foundational: clarity about what success looks like. Before an organisation can measure performance, it must define what it is measuring toward. Before it can manage performance, it needs agreed standards against which to manage.
The leadership question at each step of the sequence for building an effective PM system:
1. Define success: What does excellent performance look like in this role, at this level, in this organisation? This is defined in the earlier units of the S2R® programme.
2. Design the management system: What structure, ownership, accountability, cadence, and consequences will govern how we respond to performance data? This is the essence of this unit.
3. Design the measurement infrastructure: What gets tracked, how often, by whom, and in what format?
4. Manage using what measurement reveals: What conversations, decisions, interventions, and recognitions does this data require from us?
Why the sequence matters: Many organisations build dashboards before they have built accountability. They measure everything and manage nothing. The data exists. The conversations do not.
7: What the framework exists to do: At its core, a Performance Management system is a standardised framework, often visualised through a Performance Management Scorecard, that ensures everyone is playing by the same rules and moving in the same direction. Before examining the specific data components of such a system, it is important to understand what the framework exists to do: it bridges the gap between high-level strategy and daily habits.

A well-designed PM system must perform five distinct functions. Each function addresses a specific organisational dysfunction that, left unresolved, quietly erodes execution discipline. These five functions form the FACES framework.
Each function and the problem it solves:

F · Foster a Results Culture. Function: creates a fair and consistent environment where behaviours that produce tangible results are recognised and valued. The problem it solves: without this, organisations inadvertently reward visibility, seniority, or effort over actual results. High performers become frustrated. Underperformance is quietly tolerated.

A · Align Individual Performance. Function: creates a clear line of sight so each individual understands how their daily actions directly contribute to enterprise outcomes. The problem it solves: without this, employees are disconnected from strategy. They complete tasks without understanding which tasks actually move the needle and which ones are simply keeping them busy.

C · Create Measurement Transparency. Function: removes ambiguity in performance evaluation by making the logic, criteria, and expectations visible and understood by all. The problem it solves: without this, performance reviews feel arbitrary. Employees do not know what is being measured, how it is weighted, or what “excellent” actually looks like in practice.

E · Embed Shared Accountability. Function: ensures every Key Result or KPI is explicitly owned, making accountability visible, traceable, and non-transferable. The problem it solves: without this, Key Results are owned by committees, which means they are owned by no one. When there is no name next to a number, there is no accountability, only the appearance of it.

S · Support Continuous Development. Function: shifts performance conversations from judgement to coaching, identifying targeted areas for individual growth and capability building. The problem it solves: without this, reviews are retrospective verdicts. Leaders deliver a rating and move on. The employee leaves knowing what score they received, with no guidance on what to do differently.
8: Why the architecture is needed: To ensure the Performance Management system functions effectively, leaders must define the accountability and measurement frameworks that will monitor performance objectively. These structures ensure that performance measurement captures what was achieved, how it was accomplished, and its overall impact on the organisation’s mission.

A common framework is to set up categories of progress: progress directly contributing to Strategy advancement, progress directly attributable to Operational excellence, and progress directly attributable to cultural behaviour.

The three categories together form the PM Scorecard Architecture. They reflect a deliberate leadership philosophy: that sustainable organisational performance requires leaders who deliver results, run strong operations, and strengthen the culture simultaneously. The Three Sights of Progress ensure that the organisation rewards those leaders, and withholds that reward from leaders who excel in one dimension at the expense of the others.
These Three Sights of Progress are often given weights, either at an organisational level or at an individual level.
Purpose and typical measurement inputs of each category:

Strategy Category. Purpose: focuses on the organisation’s strategic priorities. Measures whether leaders are delivering the Key Results linked to enterprise OKRs that define the organisation’s future direction. Typical measurement inputs: strategic OKRs, cross-functional initiatives, transformation milestones, enterprise impact metrics.

Operational Category. Purpose: represents the execution engine of the organisation. Measures how effectively leaders manage the core responsibilities of their role, including quality, efficiency, and service delivery. Typical measurement inputs: department KPIs, service levels, productivity, operational efficiency, budget adherence.

Behavioural & Values Alignment. Purpose: ensures that performance is achieved in a way that strengthens the organisation’s culture and leadership standards. Evaluates whether people consistently demonstrate the organisation’s values. Typical measurement inputs: 360° feedback, demonstrated behaviours in daily interactions.
9: Why a standardised scale: To maintain objectivity within the Performance Management system, organisations use a standardised scoring scale, typically a 1 to 5 scale. This scale defines, in precise and measurable terms, what each rating represents, ensuring a common language of performance that transcends departmental boundaries and minimises individual manager bias.

Each point on the scale is clearly defined with explicit performance descriptors and criteria. This ensures that ratings are based on demonstrated evidence of performance against agreed expectations, with subjective judgement removed. The scale is applied at an individual level across all performance components, with ratings assigned based on verifiable outcomes, behavioural demonstration, and delivery against Key Results or KPIs.
By anchoring performance in clearly defined standards, the system achieves three critical outcomes:
- Personal bias is significantly reduced: ratings can be challenged and defended against explicit criteria, which take the place of managerial opinion.
- A shared language of performance is established across teams and functions: a “3” means the same thing in Finance as it does in Operations.
- Evaluation becomes consistent, comparable, and defensible, enabling fair decisions on rewards, development, and advancement.
Performance descriptor and detailed criteria for each rating:
1 · Poor: Delivery is consistently below the agreed standard. Fails to meet core expectations and requires immediate corrective action.
2 · Needs Improvement: Performance is inconsistent or variable. While some targets may be met, the individual requires active intervention or coaching to achieve the baseline standard.
3 · Meets Expectations: The “Solid Gold” standard. Consistently and reliably delivers on all agreed KPIs and behavioural expectations. This is the bedrock of organisational stability.

4 · Exceeds Expectations: Regularly delivers above standard. Demonstrates significant initiative, high-quality output, and the ability to solve complex problems beyond the immediate scope of the role.
5 · Outstanding: Proactive, self-directed, and transformative. These individuals exceed all targets and elevate the performance and morale of the teams around them.

Scoring triggers decision: For the PM system to function as a management tool as well as a measurement tool, each rating level should trigger a specific leadership response. When a rating scale is not designed to trigger a decision, it undermines the very purpose for which it was designed. Leaders read the criteria and nod. Then they do not know what to do.
Required leadership response at each rating (to read with the responses above):
1 · Poor: Immediate corrective action plan. Formal performance discussion. Clear timeline for improvement with defined milestones.
2 · Needs Improvement: Active coaching intervention. Structured support plan. Increased review frequency (bi-weekly check-ins).
3 · Meets Expectations: Sustain and recognise. Identify specific development levers to move toward a 4.
4 · Exceeds Expectations: Acknowledge contribution formally. Create stretch opportunities. Discuss advancement pathway.
5 · Outstanding: Formal recognition. Strategic deployment: leverage this person’s capability to elevate others. Succession consideration.

Facilitator note, the “Solid Gold” reframe in full: In many organisations, a rating of 3 (“Meets Expectations”) carries an unintended stigma. It is often interpreted as “average”, “ordinary”, or “just enough”. As a result, leaders may feel pressure to inflate ratings to avoid difficult conversations, while team members may feel undervalued despite delivering what is required. This interpretation is flawed and creates significant distortion in the performance management system.

The “Solid Gold” framing for a rating of 3 is a deliberate reframe. A rating of 3 represents consistent, reliable delivery against agreed expectations. It signals that an individual is meeting their commitments, maintaining standards, and contributing predictably to the organisation’s execution. This level of performance is foundational.

Organisations fail because consistent execution is missing. Strategy depends on the ability of the majority of the organisation to deliver reliably over time. Without this stability, even the strongest strategy will not translate into results, and no strategy survives contact with execution.

For this reason, a rating of 3 should be positioned as “Solid Gold”. It reflects: dependability in delivery; consistency across key responsibilities; adherence to expected standards; contribution to overall execution stability.
A small number of high performers cannot compensate for widespread inconsistency. Sustainable performance is built on a strong base of individuals who consistently meet expectations.

Leaders must therefore reinforce that: a rating of 3 is the standard of professional performance; it is the baseline required for effective execution; higher ratings (4 and 5) represent differentiation beyond this foundation and do not replace it. Reinforce this with your teams: a 3 is the foundation on which everything else is built.

When this framing is understood and applied consistently: ratings become credible and meaningful; performance conversations become honest and grounded in evidence; the organisation builds a stable execution engine capable of delivering strategy.

The impact of a calibrated system: When a performance management system is functioning correctly, the performance review becomes a no-surprise event. Because the criteria are transparent and the weighting is predetermined, team members understand exactly where they stand at any given moment. They know what is being measured, how much it counts, and what each rating means, including what leadership will do in response.
This transparency produces three powerful shifts in the organisational dynamic:

- Strategic Transparency: Every employee sees exactly how their specific contribution fuels the enterprise’s broader strategic goals. The line of sight between individual effort and organisational outcome becomes visible and motivating.

- Shift in Dynamics: The relationship between a leader and their team evolves from one of top-down oversight to one of shared investment in a common outcome. The scorecard becomes a shared tool and stops being a judgement handed down from above.
- Pathways to Excellence: The rating scale provides a clear roadmap for growth, showing exactly what is required to move from one level to the next. Ambition becomes actionable.
By anchoring ratings in clear descriptors and decision triggers, the organisation replaces subjective, instinct-based assessment with a rigorous, high-alignment framework that drives execution.
10: Where this section sits: Performance management is the intelligence layer that determines whether the high-level organisational objectives actually translate into observable progress, or whether they remain aspirational statements in a presentation deck that is reviewed at the beginning of the year and quietly forgotten by the middle of it.

Moving from strategy design to execution requires a bridge. Without this bridge, strategic goals may be intellectually coherent but operationally invisible. They exist in language that leadership understands, but that language has not been translated into the daily decisions, priorities, and habits of the people responsible for delivery.

The primary purpose of performance management is to build and sustain that bridge, ensuring that every ounce of individual effort contributes to the organisation’s strategic direction. Without it, organisations generate what might be called random acts of excellence: genuine effort, real capability, strong intentions, none of which reliably move the needle.
11: How the PM system builds the bridge: Performance management frameworks create a line of sight: a direct, visible connection between enterprise strategy and individual contribution. When this line of sight exists, performance management becomes a motivational system and stops being a compliance exercise. An employee can sit down on a Monday morning and understand precisely how their work connects to the organisation’s most critical outcomes.

Decomposing the Big Picture: Breaking each Key Result into functional measurable delivery signals: the specific, daily contributions required from every team. Strategy descends from the enterprise level to the desk level.

Defining the Logic of Success: Establishing exactly how performance is measured, where the data comes from, and which levers carry the most weight. This removes ambiguity and ensures that the rules of the game are agreed before the game is played.

Calibrating the Rhythm: Setting incremental targets so that leaders are never guessing about whether they are on track. The calculation logic is straightforward, and it tells the leadership team exactly what “on track” looks like every single month.

Structuring the Dialogue: Establishing a cadence for reviews so that performance updates become active leadership conversations: structured moments where the team asks what this data means and what to do next. A performance update is more than a data entry.
12: The S2R® position: A PM system fails when it is built solely for compliance, using pressure and monitoring to force results. The Strategy2Results® approach is built on a fundamentally different architecture: shared commitment, where the scorecard is a product of alignment and shared ownership, with no directive issued from above.
Understanding the difference between these two architectures is essential for every leader.
Five further pairs (compliance architecture first, commitment architecture second):
Imposed: OKRs and KPIs are assigned from the top down. Co-Created: OKRs and KPIs are developed through alignment dialogue; the people responsible for delivery have a voice in how delivery is defined.
Evaluative: Measurement is used to judge past failure. Educational: Measurement is used for learning and course correction.
High Pressure: Targets are set at unrealistic maximums. Execution Reality: Targets are meaningful stretches grounded in operational reality.
Retrospective: Reviews only look at what went wrong. Prospective: Reviews look back to adjust the path forward.
Isolated: Accountability sits with the individual alone. Shared: Both the leader and the KPI owner share responsibility for outcomes.

A critical point for every leader in the room: Performance Management is a leadership discipline. It is the continuous monitoring of strategic intent. When a leader delegates performance management entirely to HR, they have effectively delegated responsibility for strategy execution, and surrendered their ability to know whether the strategy is working.
13: Why the rules come first: Before cascading indicators into individual scorecards, a leader must standardise the rules of the game. This removes subjective judgement and replaces it with a data-driven framework for coaching and accountability.
Step 1 · Prepare the Foundation, the leader’s actions:
Rating Scale (select the scale): Use a numbering rating system with clear, non-negotiable descriptors. Ensure every leader in the organisation uses the same scale in the same way.
Performance Thresholds (define thresholds): Articulate in concrete behavioural and results terms what “Outstanding” actually looks like in practice, in the specific context of each role.

Evidence Standards (identify evidence): Decide now what data sources (system reports, operational audits, peer feedback, customer data) will be used to support each rating. This removes the potential for disputes later.

Review Routine (establish the routine): Set the frequency of review: monthly dashboards for operational signals, quarterly deep-dives for strategic progress, annual reviews for overall performance and development.

Step 2 · The Cascade, translating strategy to the frontline: Once the foundation is set, the leader works with the team to translate Key Results and Goals into individual delivery outcomes and KPIs. This is the cascade: the moment when enterprise strategy descends from the executive level to the individual desk. The leader’s role in the cascade is specific:

Verify the Data (verify data sources): Ensure that every measure is supported by a verifiable, system-generated or independently auditable data source. Performance cannot be managed on the basis of “gut feelings” or self-reported progress.

Assign Ownership: Every delivery goal or KPI must have a clear, named owner: a single individual who is accountable for its progress. A team, a committee or a shared responsibility cannot stand in as the owner.

Focus on Learning: Ensure that review sessions are structured around solving bottlenecks and accelerating progress. Reporting numbers to confirm they have been entered correctly does not make a review.
14: The distinction in one line: The team is measured on the quality and completion of specific activities. The leader is measured on the cumulative outcome that those activities produce.
Example: The strategic goal is to reduce complaint resolution time from 48 hours to 12 hours.
The team is measured on their daily processing speed, quality of resolution, and adherence to handling protocols.

The leader is measured on the steady, cumulative reduction in cycle time (the −0.42 hours of improvement per week) that demonstrates the strategy is gaining traction. If the team is active but the number is not moving, the leader must intervene.
15: Where this section sits: Performance management becomes fragile when success is measured in silos. If every department builds its own dashboard in isolation, the enterprise strategy dissolves into a collection of competing priorities, each legitimate within its own boundary, none of them aligned to a common direction.
16: The Brigade image: Think of the executive team as The Alignment Brigade, more than heads of departments. Every leader carries deep professional instincts about what “progress” looks like. A CFO sees progress in the margins. A CTO sees it in system uptime and deployment velocity. A CHRO sees it in engagement scores and leadership capability. These instincts are valuable, but if they are not synchronised, they create measurement imbalances that fragment the organisation’s understanding of its own performance.

The Brigade’s role is to ensure that these individual signals of success resonate together as a single, coherent enterprise system. By identifying the PM Hot Zones (the areas where each executive role naturally focuses its measurement attention), the leadership team can design a performance architecture that keeps the entire organisation moving in one direction.
17: Natural bias and alignment contribution of each role:

CEO · Enterprise Visibility. Natural bias: growth, milestones, and market position. Alignment contribution: connects the Big Picture organisational goals to functional execution signals across all departments.

CFO · Financial Signals. Natural bias: revenue, cost discipline, and ROI. Alignment contribution: links financial health to the operational drivers that create value, as well as to the outcomes they produce.
COO · Execution Rhythm. Natural bias: throughput, cycle times, and reliability. Alignment contribution: creates a sustainable and measurable pace of work that actually reaches strategic targets.
CHRO · Capability & Behaviour. Natural bias: engagement and leadership effectiveness. Alignment contribution: ensures the “how” (culture) and the “who” (skills and capability) support execution.
CTO/CIO · System Enablement. Natural bias: system reliability and digital deployment. Alignment contribution: ensures that the data used for performance management is accurate, timely, and visible.
CMO · Market Signal. Natural bias: brand awareness and customer sentiment. Alignment contribution: measures the customer journey from first contact to long-term advocacy.
CCO · Revenue Velocity. Natural bias: pipeline strength and conversion speed. Alignment contribution: focuses on long-term customer value ahead of short-term transactional results.

CPO · Supply Reliability. Natural bias: procurement efficiency and resource flow. Alignment contribution: aligns supply chain and resource availability with the organisation’s actual execution capacity.
CRO · Risk & Governance. Natural bias: compliance and operational risk signals. Alignment contribution: weaves stability and governance discipline into the way results are delivered.

CSO · Strategic Coherence. Natural bias: milestone tracking and initiative health. Alignment contribution: prevents measurement drift and keeps the enterprise anchored to the original strategic intent.
18: The risk of the isolated measure: When leadership roles stop talking to each other and begin looking only at their own functional charts, three dangerous execution gaps appear, each capable of undermining strategy delivery even when individual departments are performing well.

Gap 1 in practice: The Marketing Leader reports that leads are up and declares the quarter a success. The Operations Leader reports that the fulfilment backlog is growing and declares a crisis. The Finance Leader reports neutral margins and is uncertain what to conclude. All three are reading genuine data. None of them is reading the same story. Without an agreed enterprise progress signal, leadership conversations fragment into functional defences, and the organisation does not know whether it is winning or losing.

Gap 2 in practice: The most strategically important work often happens between departments: in the handoffs, the integrations, the coordination zones that no single function owns. If that work is not visible on any specific functional dashboard, it becomes invisible and, by default, unmanaged. What is not managed does not improve.

Gap 3 in practice: Teams will always play to the scoreboard. If the scoreboard only tracks their department’s metrics, they will optimise their own world, even when that optimisation inadvertently slows down the rest of the organisation. A sales team that closes deals without considering operational capacity creates a backlog. A finance function that optimises cost without considering capability creates a talent shortage. Misaligned scorecards are enough to produce incentive misalignment, even where intentions are good.

The leadership imperative: Performance management is a collective discipline. While each leader brings a specialised perspective to the table, the goal is to weave those perspectives into a single Source of Truth: one agreed enterprise progress signal that the entire leadership team reads and interprets together. This ensures that when the organisation says it is making progress, it means it from every angle of the business, well beyond the one angle that is performing best this quarter.
19: The shift in design logic: The design logic of performance management is evolving rapidly. For decades, organisations relied on the annual performance review as the primary mechanism for evaluating performance. That model is now being systematically replaced by Continuous Performance Management: a real-time, feedback-rich approach to monitoring and guiding execution.

Research across global organisations reveals a clear and accelerating shift, and organisations using continuous feedback structures report significantly higher employee retention. Quarterly check-ins and structured one-on-one conversations are replacing the once-a-year evaluation event.

The reason is straightforward. In fast-moving operating environments, leadership cannot afford to wait twelve months to discover that execution has drifted off course. By the time an annual review reveals the gap between strategy and delivery, months of irreversible momentum have been lost. Performance management must operate as a living system of execution monitoring: responsive, forward-looking, and cadence-driven.

Performance management in your organisation: It is highly likely that your organisation already has a formal Performance Management system in place, whether it is a global enterprise platform such as Workday or SAP SuccessFactors, a mid-market solution such as BambooHR or Personio, a specialised continuous feedback tool such as Lattice or 15Five, or a locally designed Excel-based scorecard.

Many organisations treat their PM system as a black box: data goes in, a rating comes out, and no one is entirely certain how the two are connected. When leaders understand only the mechanics of the system (which fields to complete, which buttons to click, which columns to populate), the system feels like a compliance exercise. It generates administrative burden without generating execution intelligence.

When leaders understand the logic of performance management (why the system is designed the way it is, what each component is intended to surface, and how the pieces connect to strategy), the same system transforms into a lever for clarity, alignment, and execution visibility. The question changes from “Did people complete the form?” to “Does our performance system actually tell us whether the strategy is working?” That is the perspective from which every leader in this programme must engage with their PM system.
20: The collective progress signal: The overall measure of enterprise performance is a collective progress signal. It integrates the movement of critical execution indicators across all functions into a single reference point that allows the executive team to answer one central question with shared understanding: Is the strategy advancing at the pace required to reach the intended outcome?

Without an agreed overall progress signal, leadership conversations fragment. Operations sees improvement in cycle time. Finance sees no financial impact yet. HR sees cultural progress. Strategy sees milestone completion. Each function reports progress through its own perspective, and the leadership team never arrives at a shared verdict on whether the enterprise is winning.

The Converging Zone prevents this fragmentation by creating one common interpretation of execution reality. Multiple narratives give way to a single progress signal, the agreed overall measure, that anchors every leadership dialogue about execution.
21: How the collective progress signal is used: The agreed overall measure becomes the anchor for leadership dialogue. It supports three distinct types of executive question.
Execution Traction: Is the strategy moving forward at the expected pace? Are we on track, ahead, or behind the planned trajectory?
Execution Balance: Which strategic outcomes are advancing faster or slower than the collective index? Where is the organisation accelerating, and where is it lagging?
Execution Intervention: Where should leadership attention focus to accelerate enterprise progress? Which bottlenecks require executive-level resolution?
22: Completing the design: In the Converging Zone, the leadership team completes the design of the performance management system by agreeing on how progress will be observed over time. This agreement has three elements that work together to create the execution rhythm of the organisation.
What each element answers and why it matters:

Reporting Cadence. What it answers: When do we examine execution progress? Why it matters: Without an agreed rhythm, reviews become irregular and reactive. Leaders engage with performance data only when a crisis forces the issue, by which time drift has become entrenched.

Periodic Measures. What it answers: What is the current performance level at each review point? Why it matters: Periodic measures provide the raw evidence of movement. They answer: what is the current state of execution right now? Alone, they do not show whether the organisation is progressing fast enough.

Cumulative Progress. What it answers: How far have we moved toward the target, as a percentage of the total journey? Why it matters: Cumulative progress converts periodic measurements into a trajectory signal, showing the current number together with the direction and velocity of strategic movement.

Reading the complaint resolution example: The value tells the leadership team that 22% of the strategic journey has been completed. It transforms the raw number (40 hours) into a directional signal, and triggers the leadership question: is 22% progress consistent with the time elapsed? If the organisation is 30% through the reporting period but has achieved only 22% of the target movement, the strategy is running behind pace and intervention is required.

When the three are aligned: When reporting cadence, periodic measures, and cumulative progress are aligned, the leadership team gains continuous visibility of strategy execution. Every reporting cycle answers the same central question: are we moving closer to the Success in Practice? If the answer is yes, momentum is reinforced. If the answer is no, leadership intervenes. This is the discipline that transforms performance measurement into a living system of execution intelligence.
23: Purpose of the principles: Regardless of which platform an organisation uses, an effective Performance Management system should be guided by the EXECUTION principles. These principles ensure that performance management functions as an execution intelligence system.
Further explanation and the leadership question for each principle:

E · Enterprise: Strategy First. Performance management must begin with strategic intent, and metrics follow. The first question is “What strategic outcomes must the organisation deliver?”; “What should we measure?” comes second. Measures of progress should emerge directly from Key Results. When this principle is ignored, organisations measure activity and lose sight of progress. Leadership question: Are our measures directly tied to the strategic outcomes the organisation must deliver?

X · eXecution: Line-of-Sight. A well-designed PM system creates a clear line of sight between enterprise strategy and individual contribution: from Strategy to Key Results to Operational Delivery to Individual Contribution. When this connection is visible, performance management becomes motivational and stops feeling administrative. Leadership question: Can every person in the organisation clearly explain how their work contributes to enterprise outcomes?

E · Evidence: Evidence-Based Measurement. Performance evaluation must rely on clear and verifiable evidence. Leaders must know what data source supports each measure, how frequently data is updated, and who validates it. Evidence-based measurement grounds performance conversations in data and takes opinion out of them. Leadership question: Do we have reliable and verifiable data sources for every measure we track?

C · Collective: Collective Ownership. Performance management must reinforce collective responsibility for execution. Strategy execution happens between functions as well as within them. The PM system must encourage cross-functional ownership, shared success metrics, and joint accountability. Leadership question: Are strategic outcomes owned collectively across functions, or isolated within departments?

U · Understand: Outcomes First. Performance management must prioritise outcomes over activity. Activity measures answer “Did we do the work?” Outcome measures answer “Did the work produce the intended result?” The PM system must focus on signals that reveal whether strategy is advancing. Leadership question: Are we measuring meaningful outcomes or simply tracking activity?

T · Transparent: Measurement Logic. Everyone should understand what is being measured, how it is measured, how ratings are determined, and what improvement looks like. Transparency builds trust and reduces the anxiety and perceived arbitrariness that undermine performance conversations. Leadership question: Do people clearly understand how performance ratings and evaluations are determined?

I · Incentive: Incentive Alignment. Reward structures, recognition mechanisms, and career advancement signals must align with the measures of strategic progress. When incentives contradict the measures of delivery, individuals optimise for the reward at the expense of the strategy, weakening execution discipline. Leadership question: Do our incentives reinforce the strategic outcomes and behaviours we expect people to deliver?

O · Ongoing: Review Rhythm. Performance management must operate through a consistent review cadence. Monthly reviews monitor operational signals. Quarterly reviews evaluate strategic progress. Annual reviews assess long-term performance and development. Without a defined rhythm, reviews become irregular and reactive. Leadership question: Do we have a consistent cadence for reviewing performance and strategy execution?

N · Navigate: Collective Insight. Performance data must be interpreted collectively by the leadership team. Individual dashboards provide signals, but leadership must combine those signals into a shared interpretation of enterprise progress, particularly in the Converging Zone. Leadership question: Do leadership discussions produce a shared interpretation of enterprise progress?

When these principles guide the PM process, performance management stops being a reporting mechanism and becomes something far more valuable: a leadership system for monitoring strategy execution in real time, ensuring that leaders are tracking the organisation’s movement toward its strategic destination as well as measuring effort.
25: Participant brief: You are the executive leadership team of a major hospital chain launching the MyHealth Live Portal. The system will give patients 24/7 access to diagnostic data, reduce administrative calls, and increase trust through transparency.
Outcome 1: Be the standard for fast, effortless service.
Outcome 2: Build a high-speed execution engine.
Outcome 3: Build a culture of shared ownership.
26: Short task briefs and worksheet tables (each sits with the fuller task above):
Task 1 · PM Scorecard Architecture: Design the categories your organisation will use to evaluate performance. Worksheet columns: PM Category; What Does This Category Measure?; Weight (%).
Task 2 · Scoring Logic Design: Define the performance scoring logic for your organisation. Worksheet columns: Rating; Performance Meaning; Evidence Required.

Task 4 · Reporting Cadence Design: Decide how often performance should be reviewed and provide the rationale for each decision. Worksheet columns: Cadence Option (Weekly, Monthly, Quarterly); Decision (Yes / No); Rationale.

Task 5 · Periodic Measures Selection: Define the values that will be captured at each reporting period. Worksheet: one row for each Reporting Period (Period 1 to Period 4) and one column for each of the three strategic outcomes.

Task 6 · Reporting Tool Design: Design the leadership dashboard that will track progress and calculate cumulative performance. This may be a simple Excel tool or structured Word document. Explain the calculation logic your team will use, and identify who owns each measure. Worksheet columns: Dashboard Component; Data Source; Calculation Logic / Owner.
27: Short task brief (Simulate the Baseline): Estimate the current baseline performance levels for the organisation. Worksheet columns: Strategic Outcome; Baseline, with one row for each of the three strategic outcomes.
28: The unit in summary: The Performance Management Setup unit establishes the visibility infrastructure of execution. It recognises a critical leadership reality: strategy only becomes real when progress toward its outcomes can be clearly observed, interpreted, and acted upon. Many organisations remain extremely busy yet struggle to determine whether their activity is actually advancing strategic results. Performance Management addresses this gap by creating a structured system that converts strategic intent into observable progress signals.
The unit progresses through four stages that build this capability progressively.

Awareness (What): Leaders develop a clear understanding of Performance Management as a system for monitoring strategy execution. The PM system operates as the organisational dashboard that reveals whether the work being done is moving the enterprise closer to its intended outcomes. The PM Scorecard architecture introduces a structured framework for evaluating performance across strategic priorities, operational delivery, and behavioural alignment. This architecture establishes transparency in how progress is measured and ensures that every Key Result has visible ownership and accountability.

Intelligence (Why): Leaders explore why performance measurement disciplines determine execution outcomes. Strategy and execution are connected through the performance management system; without this bridge, strategic goals remain aspirational statements and never become operational realities. The PM system decomposes Key Results into measurable delivery signals, defines the evidence required to evaluate progress, and establishes the cadence through which leaders monitor advancement. The system also reinforces a commitment-based architecture of execution, where measures of progress are developed through alignment dialogue. In this way, performance management becomes a leadership mechanism for guiding learning, adjustment, and sustained strategic momentum.

Extrapolating (Where): Leaders examine where performance management challenges most commonly emerge across the executive team. Each CXO role naturally interprets progress through its functional perspective: finance emphasises financial performance, operations prioritises throughput and reliability, technology focuses on system capability, and marketing interprets customer signals. When these perspectives operate independently, organisations develop fragmented dashboards and competing definitions of progress. The Alignment Brigade concept highlights the need for cross-CXO coordination in designing the performance architecture, ensuring that the measures of delivery across functions reinforce the same strategic direction.

Integration (Collective): The Converging Zone establishes the enterprise performance architecture. The leadership team aligns on a shared interpretation of progress by defining three essential elements of the PM system: the reporting cadence, the periodic measures that capture execution signals, and the cumulative progress indicator that shows movement from baseline toward the strategic target. These elements combine to create a collective progress signal that becomes the strategic heartbeat of execution. Through this shared signal, leadership discussions shift from fragmented functional reporting to a unified interpretation of enterprise progress, enabling the executive team to determine whether the organisation is moving closer to the Success in Practice, and where intervention is required to sustain momentum.
